chapter_theme: Songs at Sirkazhi (சீகாழி, also called Pugali, Sanbai, Kochchai, Kazhumalam and Brahmapuram): the poet confesses to courtesans who take money, to the decaying body and to delusion, and two songs voice a lovesick girl; the praise again and again makes Murugan the child-saint of Sirkazhi who sang Tamil at Madurai, cured the Pandya with holy ash and sent the Jains to the stakes.
structure_note: Courtesan songs (767, 770, 776) and the poet's infatuation (765, 769); the body (766) and royal comfort ending in ash (774); the patron-singer's shame (768, 773); praise and vows of remembrance (771, 775); akam songs in a lovesick girl's own voice (764) and another's (772), and one that folds love-sickness into the hour of death (777). The Sambandar identification runs through 766 to 769, 774 and appears in 764 (the Kaundinya son).

764.reading: In the voice of a lovesick girl, the singer says the sea, Kama's bow, the evening wind, the blame of women, the swinging bull-bells, the anril and the cuckoo come at her like fire; she melts like wax, sweats, finds musk and agil like poison, her ornaments burn to ash and her breasts pour heat, and she asks whether, his anger ended, he will not give her his honeyed, vel-adorned garland of lotus and end her longing. The praise names Uma as Bhairavi and Tripura, riding the lion and dancing with Siva among ghosts and drums, Valli who served at his feet, and Murugan the Kaundinya son of Kazhi.
764.nuance: அரிவையர் வசை, the blame of women, is the gossip (அலர்) of classical akam, set beside the anril, the cuckoo and the bull's bell. என் மாலை is probably மால், her infatuation, playing on the garland (தார்) she asks for. கவுணியர் மைந்த, son of the Kaundinyas, is Sambandar's clan name given to Murugan. The lines on Valli serving his feet among peacocks, cuckoos and parrots are hard to divide.

765.reading: The poet confesses that, maddened by the honeyed lips, breasts, slipping silk and poisonous eyes of women, he lay day after day in passion, sunk in the shade of their musk-scented hair, and asks that, worthless as he is, the great delusion this breeds come loose and grace be given. The praise speaks of the fools who do not say Hara, do not wear the holy ash, do not anoint the Lord's feet, do not learn the books of knowledge, keep to no path and weigh no dharma, rolling in the seven hells, and calls Murugan the light and full form who lives at Pugali.
765.nuance: The repeated மூடர் (written முடர் here) marks a list of the irreligious: those who do not cry அரகரா, wear திருவெணீறு or learn அறிவு நூல். கரையேற, 'to reach the shore', sits in the list in a way that leaves unclear whether these fools are the ones Murugan lifts out or the ones who fall; the reading takes the seven hells as their end. விழலன், a useless reed, is the poet's name for himself.

766.reading: The poet calls the body a bundle of flesh and skin, a stinking, pus-hot hut shaped by the four-faced Brahma who recites the Vedas, which runs, stumbles, tires, walks bent on a stick and fills with phlegm, and says he has loved this rubbish-body; he asks that the cruel diseases of the illusory world leave him and that today he be given the beautiful feet. The praise makes Murugan the teacher who at Kudal spoke Tamil books of wisdom, sent the Jain host up the stakes and with holy ash cured the fish-bannered king's fever, and who wooed Valli in the millet field and lives at Kazhi.
766.nuance: ப்ரபஞ்ச மாயக் கொடுநோய்கள்: the diseases are of the world as maya, not of the body only. The second half tells Sambandar's Madurai story in detail (ஞானத்தமிழ் நூல்கள் பகர்ந்து, சமணோர் கழுவின்கண் மிசையேற, திருநீறு, மீனக்கொடியோன்) and calls its hero குருநாதா, so the saint is Murugan himself.

767.reading: The poet describes women graceful as a bow, scented, jewelled and finely clothed, praised as matchless by ring-handed men, who tend their bodies, run many trades and will not give a man a moment without money, deceivers who do not worship the Lord's feet; fallen among them, a sinner, he asks how he can reach the shore and begs for one gift by a wonder. The praise shows the vel that turned the dark hill to dust and ruined Sura's city, the peacock, Devayanai and Valli, heralds blowing 'divine supreme guru', and the hand that gave ash and sent the Jains to the stakes at Brahmapuram, Kazhi.
767.nuance: பணமே ஒரு காசு and சற்பனைகாரர் (deceivers) mark the women as courtesans. பாதகன், sinner, and எப்படி ஓர் கரை சேர்வது set the plea as a crossing. நீறிடு கையா ... கழுவேறிட again gives Sambandar's deeds to Murugan; பிரமாபுரம் is one of Sirkazhi's twelve names. The opening lines are hard to divide.

768.reading: In tight, clipped rhythm the poet says he sang verses for men blind with drink, lust and anger, in rambling, padded words, and wore himself out for a bent and wretched gain, and asks Murugan to remove this evil. The praise tells how he sang away the fever of the Pandya Maran, against the shameless mat-wrapped Jains, and came to Kazhi, chased Valli through the thorny forest, and calls him pearl, the three fires, father, pure one, ancient one, lord of release.
768.nuance: The confession is of the patron-poet's trade, singing praise to the unworthy (கவிபாடிக் கச்சா பிச்சா), as in 245 and 773. மாறன் வெப்பு ஆறப் பாடி is Sambandar curing the Pandya's fever; பாய் சுற்று அமணர் are the Jains wrapped in mats. The compressed syllables make most of the plea uncertain.

769.reading: The poet says he was drawn by women's hair, poisoned eyes, breasts, waists, gait, words, lips and smiles, a doubter without tradition and a wretch, yet the Lord gave him by grace the sight of the two anklet-bearing feet that ended his wasted days, and this he will not forget in dream or waking. The praise shows the sea crying out and the demons' crowns broken by the vel, Murugan of Sanbai who thinks of the gods' troubles, and ends with a long abuse of the Jains as sinners without dharma and the eight thousand sent to the stakes.
769.nuance: Unusually the plea is a thanksgiving: grace has already been given (விழி அருள் தந்த பேரருள்), and the vow is கனவிலும் நனவிலும் மறவேனே. The abuse of the Jains (பறிதலை, அறநெறி பயனிலர், கழுமிசை) takes up the whole close; எணாயிரர், the eight thousand, is the number the Sambandar story gives.

770.reading: The poet describes sandal-anointed, bangled women of swan gait and deceitful minds who come close to those who give wealth, steal it with charm and spells, flare up if no gold is given now and quarrel that a month has passed without a gift, and asks for grace so that this poison and cruel poverty leave him. The praise names Murugan the nephew of the cloud-hued one who held the mountain as an umbrella for the herds in the rain, the Saravanabhava of Ambika, brother of the elephant-faced god and husband of Valli, at Sanbai where bees hum the rhythm in champaka groves.
770.nuance: நிதிதர, பொருள்கவர், செம்பொன் இங்கு இனி இலையெனில் and the month without a gift (திங்கள் ஒன்றினில் ... பொருள் உதவிலன்) make the money plain. தந்த்ர மந்த்ரிகள் accuses the women of spells. The poverty asked to be removed (கொடு மிடிமை) is the result of the courtesans. மந்தரம் குடையென is the story of Krishna lifting the hill, with the hill named Mandara.

771.reading: The poet vows never to forget, and to speak with love, Murugan's glories: the Tamil that confounded the Jains and those who said there is no faith, his grace, victory and renown, Saravana, the vel, the peacock, the feet the gods melt to worship, his gifts, and his stroking of Valli's feet and marrying her. The praise is long on Vishnu, who burnt Lanka, saved the elephant in the pool, broke the cart and the marutha trees, became the dwarf and shot at the sea, as Murugan's uncle, and ends at Brahmapuram, where Indra did penance and Guha dwells in hearts.
771.nuance: There is no confession: the plea is the vow மறவேனே, so the song is a list of what to remember. சமயமும் ஒன்றிலை என்றவரும் பறிதலையரும் sets those who deny any faith beside the Jains, both silenced by Tamil. The Vishnu catalogue gathers Rama and Krishna stories (சகடு, மருது, குறள்) into one uncle.

772.reading: In a short song in another's voice, the singer says that the moon rising from the sea like fire, the fragrant south wind and the night coming at evening have made the simple girl in love faint and stand alone, and asks Murugan to shine so that the conch-filled sea grows dim. He is the one who fights with the poison-bright vel, sweet to the words of rhythmic poets, at Sanbai.
772.nuance: The voice is a mother's or companion's (அன்புற்றெழு பேதை மயங்கித் தனியானாள்), and the classical torments of evening are the moon, the south wind and the dark. சந்தக்கவி நூலினர் may glance at the poet's own rhythmic verse.

773.reading: The poet asks Murugan to see how he stands ashamed, having wilted in mind and sung rich verses to rubbish men, calling them elephants, mountains of gold, wish-trees of giving, suns of the three worlds and treasuries of the learned; the opening tormentors, the crescent in the red sky, Kama of the cane bow, the southern wind, the vina and the gossip of mothers, are a lover's, and how they bear on the plea is unclear. The praise makes Murugan the one who taught the principle of the Veda beyond Vishnu and Brahma, split the hill and struck Sura hiding in the mango, the Muttamizh lord of Kochchai.
773.nuance: செத்தை யோகத்தினர், men of rubbish worth, and the flattering titles (கற்பதாரு, செகத்த்ரய பாநு) show the patron-poet's shame again, as in 768. The teaching of the தத்வ வேதம் to those Vishnu and Brahma could not reach is the guru-myth without Om named. The first four lines may describe the poet as a lover, or a girl's torments; the split is uncertain.

774.reading: The poet pictures a life of royal comfort: walls and mansions reaching the sun, a jewelled seat, singers on both sides, bangled women waving chowries, garlands, musk, agil and sandal paste, ruling as a king, and asks whether this body of two deeds, living in pride, should simply become a handful of ash. The praise shows Murugan taking the magic form of a vengai tree on the hill among the hunters with Valli and her friends, sending the Jains to the stakes and giving the Pandya land the ash in grace, the Kaundinya king at Kazhumalam.
774.nuance: ஒருபிடி சாம்பல், a handful of ash, is the whole of the rhetorical question; the splendour is described only to be weighed against it. வேங்கையாகி மலைமிசை தோன்றும் மாய வடிவோனே: Murugan's disguise as a tree in the Valli story. கனசமண் ... கழுமிசை தூங்க நீறு கருணைகொள் பாண்டி நாடு is Sambandar's story again.

775.reading: The praise tells how Vishnu with Lakshmi on his breast, four-faced Brahma, Indra and the sages, not having searched the Vedas, fled in fear from the warring asuras and praised Siva with garlands of song, Siva of the ash, konrai, Ganga, moon and serpent, and how by his grace the war-vel and Murugan on the blue peacock came, crossing the earth and six worlds in a moment as general of the gods. The plea asks Murugan to protect the deceiver who wanders without praising him with love as moon-faced, Kama-lovely and kadamba-garlanded.
775.nuance: The song is nearly all praise, built as a narrative of Murugan's birth for the war with the asuras; the confession is only வஞ்சனேனை, the poet's failure to praise. The lines naming the adornments of Siva's matted hair (மாதுளை, கூவிளை) and the line with corrupt characters (ஆலவ ... தரு) are hard to divide.

776.reading: The poet heaps up names for the women who sell themselves: women of love-words and coral earrings, scolders in silk, women of silent hints and quarrels, lisping talkers, pits of hell, and asks that he, bound by desire, the trickster caught in birth's sorrow, be given service at Murugan's golden lotus feet. The praise shows the vel that made the sea roar and burn and fed the sky's kites, Gauri's son, Valli embraced daily, and Murugan who rides the peacock at Kazhi and spoke into Siva's ear what Siva praised.
776.nuance: விலைமாதர், women for a price, names the trade, and the long string of -காரிகள், -சோலிகள் forms an insult catalogue in the rhythm. சிவன் மெச்சக் காதுக்கு ஓதிய: the teaching in Siva's ear, with Om not named. சேவையில் அருள்வாயே asks for service (சேவை) at the feet, not only for refuge.

777.reading: The poet says the moonlight burns like poison and the undersea fire and spreads like the sun, Kama's flower arrows wound, and on the last day, when fire boils in every direction and Death comes near to strike, he asks Murugan to come with grace and embrace him in that helpless, bewildered state. The praise shows the peacock-like Valli given by the hill people and Devayanai of the elephant, Murugan as younger brother of the elephant-faced god, son given by the mountain's daughter, Vishnu's nephew and the lord of Kazhumalam.
777.nuance: The torments of a lover (the moon, Kama's arrows) run straight into the day of death (கடைநாளில் அணுகி நமன் எற்ற), so that the lover's longing and the dying man's need meet in one request: அவசமொடு அணைத்து அருள வரவேணும். It is unclear whether the first half is the poet's own or a borrowed lover's voice.

links.note: The Naladiyar's kings who rode elephants under moon-white umbrellas were carried off and spoken of as dead; 774 gives the same royal splendour, walls, singers and chowries, and asks only whether it ends as a handful of ash.

Both are laments in another's voice for a girl sick with love for Murugan, worn down by the moon, the south wind and the evening; 772 is a bare eight lines, 24 adds the mother's question about bearing daughters.
